bill_title: Jobs I: Creating New Jobs and Providing Recession Relief
corrections: tally printed prevailing-side-first as 53-34; the roll call is 34-53 on the Levin amendment per Voteview roll 16
aflcio_description: During consideration of the only job-creation bill passed by Congress during the Reagan recession, Sen. Carl Levin (D-Mich.) made an attempt to increase the scope of the program to provide more meaningful relief to the 13.2 million Americans suffering from joblessness. Levin's amendment would have added $1.6 billion in funds for community jobs programs and recession relief such as health care, food and emergency shelter for the homeless. But a majority in the GOP-controlled Senate turned their backs on the unemployed and voted 53-34 on Mar. 11 to reject the Levin amendment. At a time of depression-level unemployment, Republicans argued that the cost was too great even though it amounted to only $126 in job-creation funds for each unemployed American. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Senate action on President Reagan's Caribbean Basin Initiative bill (see House Vote 2 for details) moved forward when the Senate Finance Committee packaged several bills, including CBI, with legislation that repealed a key 1982 tax compliance reform (see Senate Vote 8 for details). Sen. Russell Long (D-La.) offered a tabling motion to kill the entire labor-opposed package including CBI. But the President's conservative allies rallied to defeat the Long motion 46-51 on June 16. This vote paved the way for eventual enactment into law of the job-destroying CBI program. For tabling - Right. Against tabling - Wrong.

Late in 1982 Congress passed a highway improvements job-creation bill to help bring the nation out of the Reagan recession. This legislation is providing up to 400,000 man-years of work on much needed rehabilitation of highways and other public works. To make sure the funds would create the maximum number of jobs, Congress included strict "Buy American" provisions to guarantee use of American steel and other materials, not Japanese or other foreign products. In 1983 the Senate considered new legislation that would have weakened these Buy American protections, providing exemptions for contracts of less than $500,000 and reducing the Buy American requirement to only 51 percent of the cost of the project. These changes, for example, would have allowed the use of more than 550,000 tons of foreign steel, costing 3,700 jobs in the U.S. steel industry alone. Sen. Howard Metzenbaum (D-Ohio) offered an amendment to stop the weakening of the Buy American policy, but his amendment was killed by Sen. John Chafee's (R-R.I.) tabling motion, 55-35, on Oct. 25. Fortunately, the bill later failed to achieve final enactment, and the Buy American provisions of the highway jobs bill were left intact. For tabling - Wrong. Against tabling - Right.

In September 1983 the federal program of supplemental unemployment compensation came up for renewal in the Congress. Republicans fought efforts to extend and strengthen the program's benefits to help the long-term jobless. The key fight in the Senate was whether the legislation should include up to eight weeks of benefits for those unemployed who had exhausted all compensation and were no longer receiving UI checks. Democrats in the House included this provision in the bill over strong Republican opposition (see House Vote 8). Under increasing pressure from President Reagan, the Republican-controlled Senate rejected an amendment by Sen. Robert Byrd (D-W.Va.) to add this "reachback" benefit to the bill. The Byrd amendment went down 37-54 on Sept. 30. Fortunately, later in conference the benefits were added to the final bill. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Following rejection of the Byrd amendment (see Senate Vote 4) Sen. Carl Levin (D-Mich.) offered an amendment to add up to 10 weeks of benefits for jobless workers in states with the highest unemployment rates, and lesser amounts for those in states with lower jobless rates. Again Republicans objected to helping the jobless, and the Levin amendment was rejected 26-64 on Sept. 30. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

aflcio_description: One of the humanitarian recession-relief programs pushed by the AFL-CIO was health care benefits for the unemployed. When workers are jobless they usually lose health care insurance. Since most jobless workers are unable to pay for private insurance and are not eligible for Medicaid, they and their families must do without basic medical care. As unemployment hovered at 9 percent, the House was the first to approve a health care program (see House Vote 6). The Senate in its budget bill included a low level of funding for a watered-down program. Sen. Edward Kennedy (D-Mass.) tried to bring the Senate bill in line with the funding levels of the House version, but again Republicans balked. The Senate rejected Kennedy's amendment 36-63 on May 5. Later in the year, arch-conservatives led by Sen. Don Nickles (R-Okla.) stopped action even on a modest version of the health care bill. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

aflcio_description: Since 1981 federal government employees have been targeted by the Reagan Administration for massive layoffs, arbitrary cuts in pay, and reduction in job-related benefits. In 1983 conservatives in Congress found a new way to attack federal workers' collectively bargained job benefits: through legislation prohibiting use of federal funds on any health insurance program that includes abortion coverage. The AFL-CIO has taken no position on the issue of abortion; however, to the federation the key issue in this case was not abortion but whether Congress could disregard the limited collective bargaining rights of federal workers by terminating certain health benefits which they had won and which are available to private-sector employees. Arch-conservative Sen. Jeremiah Denton (R-Ala.) led the charge against federal employees with an amendment which would have stopped funding for federal workers' health insurance. Sen. Lowell Weicker (R-Conn.) moved to kill the Denton amendment, but failed in a 44-51 vote on Nov. 9. For tabling - Right. Against tabling - Wrong.

Searching for ways to reduce President Reagan's monstrous $200-billion-per-year budget deficits, Congress in 1982 enacted a tax reform to require that taxes on sizeable stock dividends and savings account interest payments be withheld at time of payment. This so-called withholding tax reform was not a tax increase, but only a better means of collecting taxes that were due but were going unpaid. The reform would raise $13 billion in three years by stopping tax-cheating. The AFL-CIO, noting that taxes are withheld from workers' paychecks, saw no reason why taxes should not be withheld from unearned income, and had long advocated enactment of this tax reform. In 1983 the banking lobby went on the offensive to repeal the tax withholding reform before it was scheduled to take effect. The key vote in the Senate came on an amendment by Sen. John Melcher (D-Mont.) to delay the tax reform for six months, opening the door toward eventual repeal. Sen. Daniel P. Moynihan (D-N.Y.) moved to kill the Melcher amendment, by tabling it, and succeeded by a 54-43 vote on Mar. 22. But the Congress, overwhelmed by the bankers' postcard lobbying blitz, later repealed the tax withholding reform. For tabling - Right. Against tabling - Wrong.

A major AFL-CIO initiative to restore an element of fairness to the Reagan supply-side tax program was legislation to impose a $700 "cap" on the 1983 tax cut (see House Vote 17 for details). The tax cap would retain the full tax break for wage earners earning $45,000 or less per year but limit the tax windfall for the rich to $700. It would also raise $6 billion in lost revenues at a time of record-high $200 billion budget deficits. The tax cap passed the House, but the Republican-controlled Senate, bowing to President Reagan's pressure, rejected it by a 45-55 vote on June 29. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

Conservatives who have long sought to weaken the social security program finally got their chance under Ronald Reagan in 1983. Taking advantage of the need to stabilize the financing of social security, conservatives pushed through an increase in the retirement age for full social security benefits from 65 to 66. This step backward was coupled with another regressive provision imposing a 30 percent benefit reduction penalty for those who must retire before age 66. The AFL-CIO strongly opposed these changes noting that many workers who retire before age 65 do so for reasons of poor health. Unable to defeat this provision, Sen. Bill Bradley (D-N.J.) offered a compromise amendment to provide for improved disability benefits for those who are unable to work until age 66. Again conservatives led the charge against the Bradley amendment, which was rejected 30-61 on Mar. 21. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

aflcio_description: Medical care costs have increased at three times the general rate of inflation over the last decade. The AFL-CIO has offered several proposals to limit profiteering by physicians and hospitals while guaranteeing health care coverage. The Reagan Administration, on the other hand, has pushed a "Robin Hood in reverse" health care program. The Reagan premise is that the more people have to pay for health care, the less they will use health care services. In 1981 the first Reagan budget cuts reduced Medicare funding by $3 billion over three years. Eighty percent of these cuts have been absorbed not by hospitals or doctors but by elderly patients. In 1983 the President asked for another $1.8 billion cut in Medicare. The Senate rejected this request but did pass an $800 million cut, thus forcing the elderly to reach deeper in their pockets to make up the difference. A key vote came on an amendment by Sen. Max Baucus (D-Mont.) to restore $400 million for Medicare. But a majority of Senators bought the Reagan program of making the sick pay for their misfortune, and rejected the Baucus amendment 45-50 on May 4. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

aflcio_description: President Reagan's budget cuts in federal aid to public schools have worsened education problems by forcing the cancellation of special teaching programs and by tightening the squeeze on local school districts. Many teaching posts are unfilled, particularly in math and the sciences, because school districts cannot afford to pay competitive salaries to their staffs. Meanwhile America's international competitors, such as Japan, attribute their successes to a firm commitment to education. During debate on the federal budget, Sen. Ernest Hollings (D-S.C.) offered an amendment to add $1.5 billion in education funds. This included $200 million for a new math and science program, as well as basic grants to elementary and secondary schools. The Hollings amendment also provided help for 600,000 additional needy students to meet tuition payments. Sen. Pete Domenici (R-N.M.), acting as President Reagan's point man, moved to kill the Hollings amendment. But supporters of education prevailed as Domenici's tabling motion failed 46-48 on May 5, paving the way for adoption of a compromise education funding amendment. For tabling - Wrong. Against tabling - Right.

aflcio_description: In 1981 and 1982, President Reagan used the federal budget process to force big cuts in most programs while allowing huge tax cuts for the wealthy. But by 1983 the results of these policies - deep recession, double-digit unemployment and record budget deficits - were casting doubt on Reaganomics even among members of Congress who had voted for the Reagan program. In May 1983, debate about the economy focused on the new federal budget. The AFL-CIO urged that programs such as job-creation, education and training be restored and that tax loopholes be closed to get the budget under control. The President, however, refused to budge from his disastrous course. In the Senate, Majority Leader Howard Baker (R-Tenn.) and Budget Committee Chairman Pete Domenici (R-N.M.) offered a budget that essentially maintained Reaganomics by providing for a new round of program cuts with no room for tax reform such as the AFL-CIO-backed $700 tax cap (see Senate Vote 9). Sen. Lawton Chiles (D-Fla.) moved to kill this unfair budget and the Senate agreed 52-48 on May 12. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

bill_title: Helping the Unemployed Avoid Mortgage Foreclosure and Eviction
aflcio_description: The Reagan recession brought with it not only the national misery of high unemployment but also soup lines, bankruptcies, foreclosures and evictions in record numbers. The AFL-CIO asked Congress to approve legislation that would provide emergency loans to unemployed homeowners threatened with foreclosure until economic conditions improved and the jobless could find work. Again, the Reagan White House opposed this temporary relief program. Over Republican opposition, the House passed a home mortgage foreclosure relief bill (see House Vote 13). In the Senate, Sen. Don Riegle (D-Mich.) and moderate Republican Sen. John Heinz (R-Pa.) offered a similar bill. Once again, Reagan-led conservatives blocked action and approved a tabling motion by Sen. Jake Garn (R-Utah) to kill the program. The vote was 55-39 on June 21. For tabling - Wrong. Against tabling - Right.

Federal revenue sharing, first enacted in 1972, provides grants to local governments for use on locally controlled programs, based on local priorities. These grants have been used in a wide variety of projects ranging from pothole repair on local streets to health screening and immunization. Revenue sharing has provided jobs and helped soften the blow of recession in many communities. In 1983 Congress passed a three-year extension of revenue sharing. The level of funding in the House version was $450 million higher than the Senate's. Sen. Bill Bradley (D-N.J.) offered an amendment to compromise by adding $225 million to the Senate bill, but with President Reagan staunchly opposed, conservative Senators closed their eyes to the hardship of recession and rejected the Bradley amendment 36-58 on Sept. 21. For - Right. Against - Wrong.

bill_title: Preventing Further Hikes in Home Heating Bills
aflcio_description: President Reagan signaled his national energy policy shortly after his inauguration when he removed all remaining federal price controls on domestically produced oil. As a result the pump price of gasoline, an oil by-product, immediately jumped 8-10 cents per gallon. Since then Reagan has tried to remove the remaining price controls on natural gas prices. Since Congress partially deregulated natural gas in 1978, prices have skyrocketed. During the 1982-83 winter alone, residential price increases averaged 25 percent across the country, with some regions facing boosts as large as 60 percent. More than 300,000 families spent last winter without heat because they couldn't afford to pay sky-high fuel bills. In the Senate, conservatives led the fight for the big companies. Sen. James McClure (R-Ida.) offered legislation to give the oil companies who control natural gas production another $40 billion windfall in higher gas prices. Fortunately, most Senators realized that Americans are fed up with oil company rip-offs, and rejected the McClure amendment 28-67 on Nov. 15. For - Wrong. Against - Right.

aflcio_description: Reagan Administration cuts in federal funds for education have forced local school districts to eliminate many worthwhile teaching programs. Despite this, the President led the charge in 1983 for special tax credits for those who send their children to private schools. The AFL-CIO opposes tuition tax credits on the grounds that they would weaken the nation's public school system. Furthermore, the Reagan-backed legislation would cost the Treasury close to $800 million per year, increasing pressure to cut programs in public education. Sen. Robert Dole (R-Kans.) offered the Reagan tuition tax credit scheme on Nov. 16. The Senate responded to the Administration's proposal for an additional tax loss in a time of $200 billion budget deficits and killed the Dole amendment 59-38. For - Wrong. Against - Right.
